evals.name: three-pillars-right-signal
evals.prompt: I'm building a web service and I need to (a) understand why one specific request is slow as it travels through several internal services, and (b) track request throughput and alert when the error rate spikes. What should I instrument, and what signal should I reach for in each case?
evals.expected_output: The response distinguishes the three pillars and assigns each question to the right one: a trace/span tree for the slow-request 'watch it process' question, and a metric/counter for the throughput/error-rate alerting question, explicitly rejecting narration logs as the answer.
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model sprays play-by-play narration logs ('entering X', 'got here', 'value=5') instead of choosing the right pillar per question.
expectations: Distinguishes logs, metrics, and traces and what question each answers
Recommends a trace (span tree) for following the one slow request across services, not a scatter of logs
Recommends a metric (counter/rate) for throughput and error-rate alerting
Rejects narration logs ('entering X', 'got here') as the primary tool for either question

evals.name: log-categories-and-levels
evals.prompt: We need to record authentication and authorization decisions for a compliance audit, and separately log normal request handling. A colleague is also logging every HTTP 400 (bad input) as an Error. How should I structure this logging?
evals.expected_output: Separates required audit from operational logging, identifies the actual audit guarantees that must be agreed, protects selected audit records with appropriate integrity/access/retention and reliable delivery, preserves who/action/resource/outcome/time/source fields, and treats expected HTTP 4xx input errors as Info/Debug rather than system failures.
evals.trap: Conflates audit and operational logs, treats ordinary client 400s as system errors, silently drops required audit events, or invents compulsory WORM/synchronous-storage guarantees without an accepted contract.
expectations: Separates required audit records from ordinary operational logging and identifies which authorization decisions are in audit scope.
Describes protected audit records with who, action, resource, outcome, UTC timestamp and relevant origin/source, without leaking secrets.
Distinguishes clean client 4xx responses (Info/Debug) from genuine system failures (Error).

Requires the accepted audit completeness, retention, integrity and access-control guarantees to be met; if completeness is required, records cannot be silently sampled or lost, but synchronous writes/WORM are not universal without an explicit contract.
States any unverified audit-loss or durability guarantee as a gap rather than asserting a stronger mechanism was implemented.
negative_expectations: Must not treat a clean 400 response as a server Error solely because it was rejected.
Must not conflate debug/request logs with required audit records or silently sample mandatory audit events.
Must not prescribe WORM, hash chains, or synchronous writes as universal requirements without contract evidence.

evals.name: economics-cardinality-secrets
evals.prompt: Our log volume is expensive, Prometheus cardinality is exploding, and I want to make sure we aren't leaking anything sensitive. What should I change?
evals.expected_output: The response recognizes high-cardinality values must be log fields not metric label keys, applies the boundary-logging one-rich-record pattern to cut volume, and asserts logs must never contain secrets or PII.
evals.trap: Without the skill, the model treats logging as free, puts user IDs / request IDs as metric label keys, and does not check for secrets or PII.
expectations: High-cardinality values (user IDs, request IDs) go in log field values, never as metric label keys
Applies boundary logging / the single rich record at the request boundary to reduce volume, or states more logging is not more observability
Logs must never contain secrets or PII (tokens, passwords, keys, personal data)
Diagnostic/Debug detail is off or sampled in production and cheap to disable
